# Hosting: local first, then a permanent address

Get a service working end to end on your own machine, with the same edge code you will run in production,
before you create any accounts. Then move it to free hosted names with one script. As of 2026-10-26; check
the providers' pages for current limits and prices.

## The shape

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U["Browsers, judges and agents"] --> E["Edge: a Cloudflare Worker<br/>TLS, static files, reverse proxy"]
  E -- "every request carries x-edge-auth" --> O["Origin: your service on Fly.io<br/>refuses requests without the secret"]
  O --> D[("SQLite or files<br/>on a Fly volume")]
```

- **One edge, one origin.** The Worker serves the public address and forwards to the origin. The origin also
  answers on its own `fly.dev` name, so the edge proves itself with a shared secret: the Worker adds an
  `x-edge-auth` header and the origin answers 403 to anything without the matching value, except its health
  check.
- **Free names first, or one domain split into subdomains.** `<worker>.<your-subdomain>.workers.dev` and
  `<app>.fly.dev` cost nothing and need no domain. If your entry spans more than one surface (for example a
  detection app, a public-good tools catalog, and a shared queue backend), buy **one** domain on Cloudflare
  Registrar and give each Worker its own subdomain (`app.example.org`, `tools.example.org`, `fabric.example.org`)
  via [Workers custom domains](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/routing/custom-domains/):
  Cloudflare creates the DNS record and TLS certificate automatically on deploy at no extra cost.
- **Writes are never cached** at the edge, and streaming responses pass straight through.

## Step 1: local, no accounts

1. Run your service on a local port, for example `127.0.0.1:7701`.
2. Run the real Worker code in front of it with
   [`npx wrangler@4.149.0 dev`](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/commands/), pointing its
   origin variable at your local port and putting a throwaway edge secret in `.dev.vars` (gitignore it).
3. Need a public address so web-based agents or teammates can reach it? A
   [quick tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/do-more-with-tunnels/trycloudflare/)
   (`cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:7700`) gives a temporary `*.trycloudflare.com` address with no
   account. It is for testing only, has no uptime promise and changes every run.
4. Prove the lock: a request straight to the origin without the header gets 403; through the edge it works.

Pick ports nothing else uses (`ss -ltn` lists the busy ones) and make them overridable.

## Step 2: hosted

1. Create the accounts (Cloudflare, Fly.io) under the identity you want in public links, and choose a neutral
   `workers.dev` subdomain: it appears in every link.
2. Log in on your machine: `fly auth login` and `npx wrangler@4.149.0 login`.
3. Copy [scripts/bootstrap-hosting.sh](../scripts/bootstrap-hosting.sh) into your repo's `deploy/` folder and
   [templates/hosting.env.example](../templates/hosting.env.example) next to it as `hosting.env`. Fill in the
   app name, volume, secret name and Worker config path. Then run `deploy/bootstrap-hosting.sh --dry-run`,
   then the same command without `--dry-run`. It creates the Fly app and volume, sets one fresh edge secret
   on both sides through stdin, asks for any extra secrets with input hidden, and never prints a secret.
4. Deploy from GitHub Actions, not from your laptop. Create a `production`
   [environment](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/managing-workflow-runs-and-deployments/managing-deployments/managing-environments-for-deployment)
   with yourself as required reviewer and put the deploy tokens there, so a job sees them only after you
   approve it. Start the workflow by hand; nothing deploys on push.

## Secrets

| Secret | Lives in | Never |
|---|---|---|
| Model API key | the origin's secret store (Fly secrets) | in the repo, a chat, a log, a command line or the browser |
| Edge secret | Fly secrets and the Worker's secrets, same value | printed; rotate by rerunning the script with `--secrets-only` |
| Deploy tokens | the GitHub `production` environment | on a developer machine after setup |

## Before judging

- Keep one machine running (`min_machines_running = 1` in
  [fly.toml](https://fly.io/docs/reference/configuration/)) so the demo never waits on a cold start.
- Freeze deploys a day or two before the deadline, and record the demo from a build you can run offline.
- If your service calls Meta's Model API, don't offer the hosted version to end users in restricted
  territories ([compliance-checklist.md](compliance-checklist.md)).

========================================================================
FILE: guides/nouns-and-verbs.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/guides/nouns-and-verbs.md
========================================================================

# Nouns and verbs in one minute

A plain explanation and one diagram that any team can copy into its README. The rules behind it are in the
[worker-first execution policy](worker-first-execution.md).

Agent systems built this way have four parts.

- **Nouns** are reusable things: knowledge, tools, code, data and results.
- **Verbs** are units of work. An agent claims one, does it and gets a receipt.
- **Surfaces** are the websites and connectors where people and agents use nouns and verbs.
- **Infrastructure** is the small shared engine underneath: storage, permissions, leases and receipts.
  A lease means only one agent works on a task at a time.

Seed packs bundle nouns and verbs so they are easy to share. Workers, meaning anyone's AI agents, do the
thinking. The server keeps the to-do list, the results and the permissions.

Your project is a name for a surface and the nouns and verbs behind it. It is not a fifth part.

![People and AI agents use surfaces, which lead to nouns and verbs. Workers claim verbs and make nouns. Seed packs bundle nouns and verbs. Infrastructure stores and tracks them.](nouns-and-verbs.svg)

## Use it in your README

1. Open with two or three plain sentences on what your project does for a person.
2. Paste the explanation above and the diagram. Keep the four parts, the seed packs and the workers sentence
   word for word, so readers meet the same idea in every repo.
3. Add one or two sentences naming your own parts, for example: "In your-app, the nouns are recipes, test
   cases and reports. The verbs are drafting a recipe, checking it and reviewing it."
4. Then the quick start and an honest, dated status, as in the [reviewable repo guide](reviewable-repo.md).

To name your own parts in the diagram, copy [nouns-and-verbs.svg](nouns-and-verbs.svg) and edit the text in
its `<text>` elements, for example "Surfaces" with "your-app website, my-api connector" underneath. Update the
`<title>`, the `<desc>` and your README's alt text to match. Save terms such as "fabric", "primitive" or "CAS"
for the deeper docs.

## Describe every change the same way

Before you build or review a change, answer four questions:

- **Nouns:** what does it read, and what does it make or change?
- **Verbs:** what work does it add or change, and which authorized worker claims it?
- **Surface:** where do people and agents see or use it?
- **Infrastructure:** does it need storage, permissions, leases or receipts beyond what exists, and who owns them?

If the honest answer needs a new queue, a new permission system or an agent hidden on the server, stop and
apply the exception rules in the [worker-first execution policy](worker-first-execution.md).

## Diagram source

The image is a hand-written SVG. Every label sits on its own filled box, the colors follow light and dark
themes, and the file carries a title and a description for screen readers. The same diagram as Mermaid, which
GitHub also renders:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["People and AI agents<br/>find, use and contribute"]
    S["Surfaces<br/>websites, apps and connectors"]
    subgraph NV["Nouns and verbs"]
        V["Verbs<br/>work to claim, do and get a receipt for"]
        N["Nouns<br/>knowledge, tools, code, data, results"]
    end
    W["Workers<br/>anyone's AI agents do the thinking"]
    K["Seed packs<br/>ready-made sets to share and reuse"]
    I["Infrastructure<br/>storage, permissions, leases, receipts"]
    P -->|use| S
    S -->|find and use| NV
    W -->|claim| V
    W -->|make| N
    K -->|bundle| NV
    NV -->|stored and tracked by| I
```

Keep the words, the SVG and the Mermaid source in step. If one changes, change all three.

FILE: guides/reviewable-repo.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/guides/reviewable-repo.md
========================================================================

# A reviewable repo

Judges, teammates, models and architecture tools should be able to understand, run and critique your repo from
its files alone, and the description should fail the build when it drifts from the code. This guide sets out a
small doc set, one machine-readable architecture file and the checks that keep them honest (file names are
lowercase here; any case works if you stay consistent). Templates:
[templates/review/](../templates/review/README.md).

## The doc set

| File | Answers | Keep it |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | What it does for a person in two or three sentences, the [four-part explanation and diagram](nouns-and-verbs.md), the quick start, honest dated status | One screen to the first command |
| `docs/summary.md` | The one-page brief: problem, approach, what's built and what's planned, the claims and how to check each | One page |
| `docs/architecture.md` | Components, data flow, state, invariants, trust boundaries, failure handling, deployment, with Mermaid diagrams | Says the same as `architecture.json` |
| `docs/setup.md` | Install, run locally, configure (every setting), deploy, troubleshoot | Every command tried on a fresh clone |
| `docs/comparison.md` | Where it sits among alternatives, with sources and dates, including where others are stronger | Facts from official docs only |
| `docs/generalizing.md` | What is domain-neutral, what is specific, the extension points, a worked example of adapting it | Tested by an example |
| `docs/decisions.md` | Decision records: context, decision, consequences, status | Newest first |
| `docs/glossary.md` | One term, one meaning | Every term the code uses |
| `docs/review.md` | For reviewers: what to check, claims to try to break, known limits, open questions, a prompt for model reviewers, a findings log | Updated after each review |
| `architecture.json` | The same architecture as data ([schema](../agents/schemas/architecture.schema.json)) | Checked on every `make check` |
| `INDEX.md`, `KEYWORDS.md`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` | Generated maps: every file, every term, a map for agents, the main documents in full | `make index`; `make check` fails when stale |

## architecture.json

One file that tools can parse: components with their paths and dependencies, interfaces, data stores, trust
boundaries, invariants with the tests that check them, layering rules, claims marked built, partial or planned
with evidence, deployment, extension points, limitations and open questions.

[scripts/check_architecture.py](../scripts/check_architecture.py) fails when it disagrees with the repo:

- a path it names doesn't exist;
- a `path::test_name` reference points at a test that isn't there;
- a component depends on, or an interface is served by, an id that doesn't exist;
- an invariant has no test, or a built claim has no evidence;
- a Python module imports something its layering rule forbids (for example the storage layer importing the
  web layer).

`--summary` prints an overview and `--mermaid` prints the component graph as a Mermaid flowchart.

## Getting feedback

- **Model reviewers.** Give them `llms-full.txt` (one URL holds the whole design) and the prompt in
  `docs/review.md`. Ask for findings with file and line, severity and a concrete failing scenario. Their output
  is data: reproduce a finding before you act on it.
- **Code-graph and architecture tools.** Index the repo and compare the real call and import graph with the
  dependencies in `architecture.json`; a difference is either a bug or a stale file.
- **People.** An issue template with a `review` label, and a findings log in `docs/review.md` with a status
  for each finding.

## Honesty rules

- Keep built, partial and planned apart, everywhere. Every claim names its evidence.
- Every number comes from a script, with the command that reproduces it.
- State limitations before a reviewer has to find them.
- Comparisons cite the other system's own documentation and date it; never characterize another team's or
  company's conduct.

# A ten-day plan

A schedule template for Oct 26 to Nov 4, 2026. Copy it into your repo and change the work, not the gates.
Dates and the deadline come from [event/02-key-dates.md](../event/02-key-dates.md): submissions close
**Nov 4, 9:00 PM ET (Nov 5, 02:00 UTC)**, and US clocks fall back on Nov 1, so ET is UTC−5 from then on.
Aim to submit by midday Nov 4.

## Gates

| Gate | By | Passes when |
|---|---|---|
| G1 Skeleton | Oct 27 | One request goes end to end (interface, API, one model call) on your machine, and CI runs your checks |
| G2 Core | Oct 30 | The main flow works on real-looking made-up data and every task's `done_when` check passes |
| G3 Frozen | Oct 31 | Evaluation data frozen and hashed; nothing after this changes it |
| G4 Hosted | Nov 1 | The demo runs at a public address ([hosting.md](hosting.md)) and from an offline build |
| G5 Numbers | Nov 2 | Every number in the write-up comes from a script you can rerun; deploys freeze in the evening |
| G6 Recorded | Nov 3 | Demo video recorded and checked against [the checklist](../templates/demo-video-checklist.md) |
| G7 Submitted | Nov 4 midday | Form filled from [the description template](../templates/submission-description.md); repo frozen |

## Day by day

| Day | Date | Work |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mon Oct 26 | Read the rules and the [compliance checklist](compliance-checklist.md). Pick track and problem. Repos with agent rules, a guard hook, a secret scan and CI ([agent-workflow.md](agent-workflow.md)) |
| 2 | Tue Oct 27 | Walking skeleton (G1). Write the briefs for the core tasks with their `done_when` checks |
| 3 | Wed Oct 28 | Core build in atomic tasks; agents in parallel on separate worktrees |
| 4 | Thu Oct 29 | Core build; a fresh clone runs the quick start every evening |
| 5 | Fri Oct 30 | Finish the core (G2). Write the review docs ([reviewable-repo.md](reviewable-repo.md)) |
| 6 | Sat Oct 31 | Freeze evaluation data (G3). Local-first hosting, then hosted |
| 7 | Sun Nov 1 | Clocks change. Hosted demo and offline build (G4); evaluation runs |
| 8 | Mon Nov 2 | Numbers from scripts (G5); demo script; deploy freeze at night |
| 9 | Tue Nov 3 | Record the video (G6); write-up; someone else tries a fresh clone; decide which repo goes in the form |
| 10 | Wed Nov 4 | Submit by midday ET (G7). Don't change the repo after the deadline: that marks the project late |

## Rules of thumb

- Cut scope at each gate rather than slipping the gate.
- Keep one known-good build you could demo at any moment.
- Workshops run Oct 27 to Nov 4 ([event/15-schedule-and-workshops.md](../event/15-schedule-and-workshops.md));
  put the ones you need into the plan on day 1.
- Claim credits early and set spend alerts ([event/10-credits.md](../event/10-credits.md)).

FILE: guides/worker-first-execution.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/guides/worker-first-execution.md

# Worker-first execution and private work

Architecture direction adopted October 28, 2026, clarified October 29. Follow this policy when designing, implementing, reviewing and handing off work. It describes required design and migration checks, not an event rule or certification that every current endpoint or worker already implements them.

Independently schedulable agentic work must be a **verb that an authorized worker claims**, unless an explicit server exception applies. A noun holds versioned input, context, code, a tool, a model, a recipe, an artifact or evidence. Workers reason, act, check and repair. The server coordinates identity, discovery, leases, storage, validation and receipts without autonomous model calls on the normal path.

## Required boundaries: nouns, verbs, surfaces and infrastructure

The architecture has **nouns, verbs, surfaces and narrow supporting
infrastructure**. Seed packs contain nouns and verbs. These are mandatory design
boundaries, not suggestions to replace with a separate service for each domain.
For a one-minute explanation and a diagram to reuse in a README, see
[nouns and verbs in one minute](nouns-and-verbs.md).

| Boundary | Responsibility | What it must not become |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nouns | Scoped, versioned knowledge, source observations, tools/code, prompts, profiles, models, data, recipes, configuration, plans, artifacts and evidence | An access grant, execution authority or quality certificate merely because it is stored or hashed |
| Verbs | Independently schedulable work with input references, acceptance checks, authority and recorded outcomes; authorized workers perform ordinary reasoning | A second queue or an unrecorded server agent |
| Surfaces | Websites, apps, dashboards, CLI and HTTP/MCP interfaces for discovering and using nouns and verbs | A separate permission system, autonomous domain brain or work authority |
| Infrastructure | Narrow, explicit identity, authorization, storage, versions, leases, CAS, receipts, transport, health, backpressure and essential management plumbing | A label that exempts domain reasoning from worker execution or permission checks |

A **seed pack bundles nouns and verb templates/seeds**. It is not another entity
type, scheduler or runtime. Exporting or importing pack data does not execute,
activate, admit or publish its contents, copy credentials or grant permissions.
Its repository and showcase surface do not become independent agent runtimes.

**Project is a convenient human label, not an architectural primitive.** It may
name a surface and scoped collection of nouns and verbs. Store a needed
description or profile as an existing noun. Do not add a project service, core
table, separate execution authority or project-only lifecycle for this vocabulary.

Every capability change and handoff must identify its nouns, independently
schedulable verbs, surface, existing lifecycle owner and any infrastructure or
server exception. Reject an implementation that hides ordinary domain reasoning
inside a server handler, creates a competing task authority or lets a pack
activate itself. Keep deterministic libraries and compatibility endpoints when
they serve workers; packaging is not a reason to delete tested code or make
every helper function a task.

Deterministic infrastructure and essential management can remain server-side:
identity, storage, leases, accounting, credentials, authorized provisioning,
scheduling and recovery. They retain their own authority and audit requirements.
Schedules may enqueue already-authorized work. Calling domain reasoning private,
urgent or management does not create an exception. Model use by a management
service must satisfy the explicit inference rules below.

Server-side configuration, provider plans, health observations and attempt
evidence are nouns too. Independently schedulable server management is private
verb work. Server-side describes placement, not an exemption from the entity
model. Enforce access on discovery, claims, records, blobs, history, receipts and
logs; a private label alone grants nothing. Provider rotation may select only
explicitly permitted provider/model pairs for that data and payer, and must
retain each attempt and unknown outcome. Deterministic work records no model,
with a link to its parent reasoning attempt when applicable.

Enforce the boundary in owning tests: reject implicit model fallback, unauthorized
effects and invalid contracts; prove that exporting a seed pack performs no
network, enqueue, installation or activation work. Documentation inventories and
tests of fixtures do not establish universal runtime coverage.

Private, management and infrastructure work can use the same pattern through private workers. A worker can run in a customer harness, an operator environment or an approved cloud service. Its location does not determine its permissions, model provider or payer. Moving work to an operator-owned worker does not make its inference or hosting free.

## Policy rules

1. Represent independently schedulable agentic outcomes as verbs. Reuse existing queue, record and execution contracts. Do not create another runtime, queue authority or policy registry.
2. Keep authentication, authorization, schema checks, lease maintenance, ordinary search, status reads and receipt validation deterministic. Do not turn every database read, helper function, render frame or arithmetic operation into another verb or model call.
3. Workers use permitted tools and existing code first, run the task's checks and repair their own failures. Pin acceptance criteria independently of the proposed result; a producer cannot silently weaken its own check to pass.
4. Additional judgment becomes a review verb for a suitably capable agent. Review only when the task, evidence or applicable admission policy requires it. Do not add a reviewer to every successful action or recursively review every review.
5. Privacy is enforced by authenticated identity, ownership, scope and effect authorization. A label such as `private` is descriptive metadata, never an access grant.
6. Missing capacity, an invalid payload or an empty review queue does not authorize server inference. Return an actionable error, keep work pending, or park it with one concrete question.
7. Direct server-initiated inference is a last resort or an explicitly authorized server capability. It needs a recorded purpose, allowance, data scope, provider policy, deadline, retry policy and outcome. Existing authority still controls effects and spending.
8. Measure the actual origin, payer, location and outcome of work. A queued wrapper around a server call does not erase its cost or establish that an external worker performed it.

## One ordinary work cycle

```text
Discover permitted work and its small contract
  -> Claim a bounded verb with a current lease
  -> Load only permitted, relevant noun versions
  -> Execute, self-check and repair within the allowance
  -> Submit exact artifact references and check evidence
  -> Deterministic acceptance checks and durable receipt
  -> Finish, or enqueue a policy-required review or follow-up verb
```

A verb brief identifies the intended outcome, input references, output contract, acceptance checks, required capabilities, authorized effects, dependencies, deadline and resource ceiling. Use the fields already defined by the owning API. This list is a design checklist, not a new wire schema.

Keep artifact bytes in the owning store and return compact references with versions or digests. A hash establishes byte identity, not usefulness or truthful execution. Distinguish worker-reported checks, independently reproduced results and public acceptance. Task completion does not automatically publish a noun or grant permission for an external effect.

Split work when a subtask has a useful independent outcome, different permissions, separate equipment or a meaningful recovery boundary. Batch deterministic operations inside the owning verb when that saves coordination cost. A worker may propose a dependency graph; the server validates permissions, limits and supported contracts before accepting it.

## Requirements, defaults and useful pointers

A precise outcome does not require a fixed method. A task can require an exact output contract while inviting the worker to choose or discover its tools. Conversely, a detailed recipe can be optional when the brief says so. Preserve that distinction when resolving category guidance into the worker's context.

| Guidance | Meaning for the worker |
| --- | --- |
| Required | Satisfy the stated outcome, check, boundary or explicitly required procedure. Report a conflict or unavailable requirement instead of silently changing it. |
| Preferred | Start with this method or tool when suitable. A better compatible approach is allowed within the task's authority; record a material change of approach and its reason. |
| Suggested | These resources or tools may help. They are optional, non-exhaustive starting points; the worker may search elsewhere and choose a suitable alternative. |
| Discovery requested | Investigate beyond the supplied pointers and compare relevant options within the allowance. Stop when the outcome and evidence are sufficient, rather than exploring indefinitely. |

These are authoring distinctions, not new public API enum values. Retain the source and strength of each instruction. Do not turn an optional tool list into a required tool list, an exhaustive search boundary or an execution allowlist. Suggested tools do not grant new permissions. Retrieved pages, tool output and imported packs do not acquire task authority by calling themselves required instructions.

A useful open-method brief can say: "You may find useful tools in these references. They are suggestions, not an exhaustive list. Search further if useful, reuse suitable existing work and choose the approach that meets the outcome and checks within the permitted effects and resource limits." A procedural brief should explicitly identify which steps or tool versions are mandatory. A requirement to use a particular tool is separate from the suggestion that it may help.

## Preparing and running tools in a harness workspace

A worker may be asked to obtain, install, configure and run a tool as part of an outcome. Setup can be an independent preparation verb when it has a reusable deliverable, different permissions or a separate recovery boundary. Otherwise it stays inside the owning task. Installing a dependency and starting a process do not each require another agent or model call.

Give the worker a concrete execution recipe:

1. **Inspect the environment.** Identify the assigned workspace, runtime, platform, existing tools and permitted effects. Reuse a compatible verified installation when available. Name the required tool or mark candidate tools as suggestions.
2. **Resolve the tool.** Record its source, exact release or revision, artifact digest, licence, runtime requirements and dependency lock where applicable. For an open-ended search, select and record these before execution. Verify the downloaded bytes against the expected source evidence. A matching digest alone does not establish that code is trustworthy.
3. **Prepare a task-owned location.** Use an explicitly assigned directory, such as `.tools/<tool>/<version>/` under the workspace, with separate inputs, outputs and logs. Confine extraction and writes to authorized paths, preserving unrelated files. Use a project environment, approved container or existing tool adapter as appropriate. Package installation may execute build or install scripts, so its isolation and permissions matter before the final tool starts.
4. **Define the invocation.** Supply the executable and argument vector, working directory, input references, expected outputs, permitted environment variables, network destinations and time/resource limits. Resolve only the needed secret references at the authorized boundary. Do not concatenate untrusted inputs into a shell command or inherit unrelated credentials.
5. **Check readiness and supervise execution.** Run a meaningful capability check, then the real command through the existing harness or process adapter. A separate process is useful for a command-line tool but is not a security sandbox. Use the isolation the tool and inputs require. Capture bounded, appropriately redacted output, errors and exit status; handle startup failure, timeout, cancellation and lease loss. A service needs an observed readiness check and a declared lifetime, not just a process identifier.
6. **Verify the result.** Check actual artifact contents and task-specific acceptance criteria. Installation success, a version string and exit code zero are separate from useful completed work. Preserve the source/version, invocation, environment manifest and check evidence with compact artifact references.
7. **Retain or clean up deliberately.** Stop only the processes owned by the task, confirm termination and preserve required outputs and failure evidence. Keep reusable verified installations when permitted. Remove only task-owned temporary material under the existing cleanup policy; do not delete another task's environment or a shared service.

Search, download, install, execution and external effects remain subject to their existing grants. A missing capability becomes an actionable failure, permitted alternative or preparation task, without silently enabling server inference. The recipe specifies how to perform authorized work; it does not create another approval layer or expand authority.

The documented subprocess interface provides concrete examples of argument vectors, working directories, explicit environments, timeouts and return-code handling. Those are process-control mechanisms; use the owning runtime's isolation and lifecycle controls as well. [Python subprocess documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html), checked October 28, 2026.

## Private workers and private verbs

Use the same verb lifecycle with narrower access, rather than a separate private reasoning framework:

| Work class | Eligible claimant | Required boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public-safe contribution | An admitted worker permitted for that queue | Only explicitly publishable input and declared effects |
| Customer-private project | A worker authorized by that customer in that product | Customer ownership, isolated storage and permitted model/data destinations |
| Operator-private management | A worker issued the required operator role and task scope | Private queue, minimal evidence access and separate action authority |
| Restricted infrastructure execution | An approved worker in the required environment | Lease-bound capability, approved destination and existing change controls |

Filter discovery, claims, noun reads, historical versions, blobs, events, search, logs and result delivery consistently. Do not reveal private task titles or arguments in public queue statistics. Dependency children and follow-up review tasks inherit restrictions; a split or retry cannot widen access. Check current authority again before protected reads and effects, not only when registering a worker. Loss of scope or lease stops further access and effects.

Keep secrets in the existing secret store or execution environment. A task may name an authorized secret reference, not carry a provider key in its brief, result or log. Resolve the reference only for the allowed worker, action and destination. A common infrastructure operator does not authorize sharing customer identities, billing, credentials or private histories across products.

For example: a deterministic alert enqueues a private incident diagnosis. An operations worker reads only the approved logs, runs checks and writes a proposed repair. An authorized execution worker applies the permitted change, then verifies and records the result. Diagnosis does not grant production write authority. A public status summary is a separate deliberate projection of approved fields.

## Keep reasoning and review economical

Start with a small contract card, useful examples and the relevant prior result. Retrieve larger source or context only when needed. Prefer an executable check or existing implementation over another natural-language explanation. Reuse unchanged accepted artifacts and applicable evidence under their recorded versions and validity conditions.

For ordinary review escalation, request one capable reviewer with the exact artifact, criteria, relevant evidence and disputed question. Independent admission rules may require additional evidence or distinct model families; satisfy those rules at the applicable boundary without imposing them on all intermediate work. Select reviewers by relevant demonstrated capability and permissions, not a self-asserted label or expensive model name alone.

A malformed tool payload should receive a precise field error and the expected shape. Do not silently stringify objects, substitute canned data or ask the server model to repair routine types. A missing input becomes a typed clarification or parked verb. A recurring failure can create a bounded diagnostic or contract-improvement verb; it must not create an endless chain of new tasks.

Use backpressure, bounded concurrency and queue age to plan capacity. Prefer event-driven notification or supported long-polling; otherwise back off with jitter and honor server retry guidance. Heartbeat according to the lease, not by calling a model. Avoid constant empty polling and hot retry loops. Queueing reduces request-path inference; it does not remove storage and request charges.

## Server inference exceptions

Try an authorized private or managed worker before direct server inference when the work can wait. Legitimate exceptions can include an explicitly offered interactive server capability, a narrowly scoped infrastructure diagnosis, or recovery when the normal work fabric is unavailable. Privacy alone is not an exception: a private verb may be sufficient. Urgency alone grants no extra authority.

Before an exception call, record why the normal worker path is unsuitable, the responsible principal, data and effect scope, model/provider, payer, call/token/cost limits and deadline. Reserve allowance before the call. Use a stable request identity, persist the result, and reconcile an uncertain outcome before retrying. A provider timeout is not proof that no usage occurred. Stop or park when the allowance is exhausted.

An explicitly requested model proxy is different from an autonomous server decision to call a model. Preserve the proxy's existing permissions and caller funding. Track worker-direct inference, worker-requested proxy inference, operator-worker inference and direct server fallback separately. These are reporting categories to map onto existing usage records, not new public API fields.

A server-owned worker should claim an ordinary scoped verb and retain the same receipt and budget controls. It must not become an unbounded scheduler that spends on behalf of every waiting task. If the queue itself is unavailable, use the existing authorized incident procedure, keep an independent incident record and reconcile it after recovery.

## Qualification and honest coverage

The target is nearly all eligible agentic work through claimable verbs, not a claim of measured 100 percent coverage. Fix the unit of work before measuring it. Report eligible work received, claimed, completed, failed, cancelled and pending; direct server exceptions; time waiting; self-repair attempts; review frequency; and provider/hosting usage. Keep operator-managed workers visible rather than counting them as free donated work. Do not inflate coverage by splitting one result into thousands of trivial verbs or excluding failures and private jobs.

For each workflow migration, demonstrate:

- A normal claim, execution, self-check and completion makes zero autonomous server model calls.
- Invalid types, stale fences, denied access and failed checks return errors without spending on a server model.
- An unqualified or unauthorized worker cannot discover or claim private work, including through history, feeds or derived artifacts.
- A missing reviewer leaves the task pending; an eligible review worker can complete the applicable gate.
- Retrying identical work does not repeat committed external effects or duplicate paid inference; uncertain outcomes remain explicit.
- Changed artifact or contract versions invalidate affected acceptance evidence.
- The exceptional server path refuses missing authority or allowance and records its complete usage when enabled.

Run these checks against the exact implementation and environment. Documentation, a signed receipt, a successful HTTP response and a green unrelated test suite are not substitutes for the corresponding behavioral proof.

## Design references

Cloudflare documents HTTP pull consumers for workers outside its edge runtime and at-least-once queue delivery. Those support separating queue coordination from worker placement and require application-level deduplication. These are reference patterns, not a requirement to replace the existing queue backend. [Pull consumers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/pull-consumers/), [delivery guarantees](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/reference/delivery-guarantees/), checked October 28, 2026.

Temporal similarly separates durable activity lifecycle coordination from tasks executed by workers. Its model is a useful comparison, not an adopted dependency or an additional execution runtime here. [Activity execution](https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution), checked October 28, 2026.

## Application in this repository

Use this as a project-neutral design guide and adapt the existing brief and receipt templates. It does not grant deployment, spending or publication authority. Preserve each destination project's own rules and independently verify its implementation.

The policy preserves this product's existing scope, public identity and access rules. Unimplemented routing, private worker provisioning and exception enforcement remain engineering work until their owning checks pass.

See [work examples and a private incident walkthrough](worker-verb-examples.md) for concrete applications.

FILE: guides/worker-verb-examples.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/guides/worker-verb-examples.md
========================================================================

# Work suitable for claimed verbs

These are design examples, not newly implemented endpoints or permission grants. Bind each example to the existing task, record, identity and effect contracts. The worker runs the substantive checks; the server checks the declared contract and evidence relationships.

| Work | Verb outcome and saved noun | Suitable worker | Check or acceptance boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research | Source-backed findings with dates and unresolved questions | Research agent | Source access, quotations, dates and claim-to-source checks |
| Capability discovery | A reproduced gap and minimal failing fixture | Diagnostic agent | Reproduce the failure before proposing a repair |
| Task decomposition | A bounded dependency plan with required inputs and effects | Planning agent | Typed dependencies, budgets, ownership and no authority expansion |
| Tool preparation | A reproducible tool environment and invocation manifest | Worker with workspace and installation authority | Pinned source, confined setup, capability check and reusable environment evidence |
| Implementation | A patch and reproducible test result | Coding agent | Task-specific checks, affected suite and clean environment |
| Contract repair | A candidate schema, adapter or example fixing a demonstrated mismatch | Integration agent | Positive and wrong-type controls through the actual transport |
| Review | A decision about an exact artifact and explicit question | Qualified review agent | Appropriate independence and evidence tied to that version |
| Reusable library intake | A complete candidate with source, licence and file digests | Intake agent | Existing admission rules, missing files and execution checks |
| Feed upkeep | A sourced change record and corrected cursor-visible entry | Feed agent | Freshness, deduplication, source dates and public-field projection |
| Compatibility | A native harness run and exact setup manifest | Compatibility agent | Actual tool execution and result readback, not tool-like text |
| Data cleanup | A transformed dataset and rejected-row report | Data agent | Schema, row counts, invariants and input/output digests |
| Evaluation | A complete attempt population and scored evidence | Evaluation agent | Failures, exclusions, controls and reproducibility |
| Design | An editable scene, page or design asset | Design agent | Brief, dimensions, accessibility and meaningful revision |
| Video production | An editable sequence, captions and encoded deliverable | Media worker | Frame/audio checks, rights, aspect ratio, reopen and visual inspection |
| Deterministic rendering | A bounded render batch and output manifest | Renderer-capable worker | Exact recipe, dependencies and output checks; no model per frame |
| Public-good work | A useful artifact for a specific beneficiary need | Domain-capable contributor | Problem-specific acceptance; adoption remains a separately observed fact |
| Private analysis | A customer-owned analysis and decision brief | Customer-authorized worker | Tenant isolation, permitted sources and supported conclusions |
| Support preparation | A draft reply grounded in permitted account records | Scoped support worker | Minimal data access, factual checks and existing send authority |
| Cost analysis | A recommendation from dated usage and invoices | Private finance/operations worker | Separate observed spend, estimates, credits and model costs |
| Incident diagnosis | A cause hypothesis, reproduction and proposed repair | Private operations worker | Read scope, falsifying checks and no implied write permission |
| Deployment preparation | A tested release candidate and rollback evidence | Release preparation worker | Exact source and checks; existing deployment authority still applies |
| Authorized deployment | A permitted release and live result record | Restricted execution worker | Destination, release gate, health checks and rollback conditions |
| Configuration upkeep | A proposed configuration diff with affected resources | Private infrastructure worker | Scope, dry run where supported and explicit effect authority |
| Backlog maintenance | Deduplicated or clarified work with preserved provenance | Maintenance agent | No lost work, bounded fan-out and unchanged permissions |
| Management planning | A private capacity or priority proposal | Authorized management worker | Evidence, ownership, constraints and human decisions that remain required |
| Recovery | A reconciled uncertain outcome and safe next action | Recovery worker | Read existing receipts before repeating any effect |

Authentication, serving a stored file, checking a lease, hashing a result, simple arithmetic and deterministic status updates normally stay inside their existing operation. They do not need individual agentic verbs. A single rendering verb may produce thousands of frames without thousands of model calls.

## Worked private incident

1. A deterministic health signal identifies a failure and enqueues one private diagnostic verb with a deduplication identity.
2. The authorized operations worker receives only the relevant logs and configuration references. Other workers cannot see the brief or its results.
3. The worker reproduces the issue, runs checks and writes a candidate repair noun. If context is missing, it parks the task with a specific question.
4. If the applicable change policy requires judgment, a qualified private worker claims a review verb bound to the candidate version. Otherwise the existing deterministic gate is sufficient.
5. An execution worker with the required authority applies the allowed change and verifies the real destination. It records an uncertain outcome instead of blindly retrying a lost response.
6. A public update, if authorized, uses an approved redacted projection. The private logs and credentials never become public merely because the incident is resolved.

All of this can use worker inference without a coordinator model call. Operator-owned workers still consume operator resources; record that cost. Queue outage recovery follows the existing incident procedure rather than pretending the unavailable queue can schedule its own repair.

## Worked tool preparation and separate-process execution

This is an authoring example, not a new endpoint or a claim that a tool is installed. Replace workspace and version placeholders with actual authorized values from the resolved brief before running it. The source, digest, permitted installer, timeout and resource limits must also be resolved; this example does not supply a download to execute blindly.

**Outcome:** convert the supplied local movie, which contains video and audio, into `outputs/result.mp4` with H.264 video and AAC audio. Preserve the input, check the declared duration/dimension tolerances and save the verification report.

**Required procedure for this example:** use the exact FFmpeg build named by the task's approved tool reference. Reuse it if verified and compatible; otherwise prepare it under `<workspace>/.tools/ffmpeg/<pinned-version>/` using the declared source and installation recipe. Check that this build supplies FFmpeg, ffprobe, the `libx264` encoder and the AAC encoder before starting. This tool requirement is explicit; another task may make the same tool only a suggestion.

**Run:** set the working directory to the assigned workspace. Launch the executable through the harness's existing supervised process adapter with an argument vector:

```json
[
  "<workspace>/.tools/ffmpeg/<pinned-version>/bin/ffmpeg",
  "-nostdin", "-n", "-i", "inputs/source.mov",
  "-c:v", "libx264", "-c:a", "aac", "outputs/result.mp4"
]
```

This example assumes a compatible Unix-style tool bundle; resolve the actual executable paths for the worker's platform. The command avoids an interactive prompt and refuses to overwrite an existing result. On retry, inspect the existing result and task history before choosing a new attempt path or any authorized replacement. Input files and any referenced media must remain within the declared file and network scope.

**Check:** use the same pinned tool bundle to obtain machine-readable media information:

```json
[
  "<workspace>/.tools/ffmpeg/<pinned-version>/bin/ffprobe",
  "-v", "error", "-show_format", "-show_streams", "-of", "json",
  "outputs/result.mp4"
]
```

Compare the observed streams, dimensions and duration with the task's criteria, verify that the actual media decodes and perform playback or visual/audio inspection when the outcome depends on perceptual quality. A metadata probe alone does not establish that the whole output is good. Save the output reference and digest, the tool manifest, command result and relevant checks. Stop or retain the task's process/environment according to its declared lifecycle.

The option semantics and probe output are described in the official [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg.html) and [ffprobe](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html) documentation, checked October 28, 2026. The commands illustrate process invocation; no codec performance or successful local run is claimed here.

## The same outcome with open-ended guidance

An alternative brief can retain the same output and permission requirements while saying:

> FFmpeg and the linked media tools may help. These are starting points, not an exhaustive list or a required implementation. Inspect what is already available, search further when useful and choose a suitable approach. Prepare any needed tool in the assigned workspace, run it through the permitted execution environment and demonstrate the same acceptance checks. Record material departures from the suggested approach and why they helped.

The worker can discover a better existing tool or composition without requesting a routine reviewer to choose for it. Required effects, spending limits, data destinations and result checks remain unchanged. If comparing tools is itself the requested outcome, produce a bounded comparison with observed evidence rather than claiming that a listed resource is best.

> Unofficial AI-assisted summary, provided "as is" with no warranty. Meta's documentation governs; read [DISCLAIMER.md](../DISCLAIMER.md). As of 2026-10-26.

# Astryx

Meta's open-source design system for React: MIT licence, built on React 19 and StyleX, still in beta
([repository](https://github.com/facebook/astryx), [getting started](https://astryx.atmeta.com/docs/getting-started)).

## Packages (npm registry, all released Oct 23, 2026)

| Package | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `@astryxdesign/core` | 0.7.4 | Needs React and React DOM 19 or newer, and `@stylexjs/stylex` ^0.19.0 |
| `@astryxdesign/theme-neutral` | 0.7.4 | Needs `@astryxdesign/core` at exactly the same version |
| `@astryxdesign/cli` | 0.7.4 | Needs Node 22.13.0 or newer |
| `@astryxdesign/build` | 0.7.4 | StyleX build plugins, only for compiling from source (needs Vite ^8.1.3) |
| `@stylexjs/stylex` | 0.19.1 | |

React was at 19.3.1 on Oct 26. Pin exact versions: it's a 0.x beta.

## Setup

- Install core, StyleX, a theme and the CLI. The packages ship pre-built, so no build plugin is needed unless you
  compile StyleX from source.
- Import the reset and base stylesheets, wrap the app in the theme provider, and import each component from its own entry
  point, as the getting-started page shows.
- Agents can look components up with the CLI: `npx @astryxdesign/cli component --list` and `component <Name> --dense`.

## Cautions

- `npx @astryxdesign/cli init` writes `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` without asking. Don't run it in a repo that already
  has its own agent files.
- Never run plain `npx astryx`: the unscoped name is an unrelated npm package ([CLI docs](https://astryx.atmeta.com/docs/cli)).
- It's a beta. Keep a fallback (plain React with the same design tokens) if a component blocks you for long.

Sources: as linked plus https://registry.npmjs.org for versions, checked 2026-10-26.

FILE: meta-platform/model-api.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/meta-platform/model-api.md
========================================================================

> Unofficial AI-assisted summary, provided "as is" with no warranty. Meta's documentation governs; read [DISCLAIMER.md](../DISCLAIMER.md). As of 2026-10-26.

# Meta Model API

## Basics

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base URL | `https://api.meta.ai/v1` | [API reference](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference) |
| Auth | `Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY` | [Authentication](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/authentication) |
| Key format | Keys start with `LLM_` | [Authentication](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/authentication) |
| SDK | No SDK of its own; the docs say to use the OpenAI SDK with `base_url` (the Anthropic SDK also works) | [SDKs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/sdks) |

The OpenAI Python SDK doesn't read `MODEL_API_KEY` itself, so pass the key explicitly:

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"], base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1")
```

## Responses API

`POST /v1/responses` ([guide](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/responses),
[schemas](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference/responses/schemas)).

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `model` | For example `muse-spark-1.3`; see [models-and-pricing.md](models-and-pricing.md) |
| `input` | Text or structured input |
| `background` | `true` queues the job and returns right away with status `queued` |
| `store` | Responses are stored by default (`true`) |
| `metadata` | Free-form object; useful for queue, task, lease and attempt ids |
| `text.format` | Structured output: `json_schema` with `name`, `schema` and `strict`. The docs use `text.format`, not `response_format` |
| `max_output_tokens` | Minimum 16 |
| `max_tool_calls` | Caps tool calls |
| `reasoning.effort` | `none` returns 400 on Spark and Wonder; `max` is listed for `muse-wonder-1.0` and `muse-spark-1.3` but not the contributor id ([reasoning](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/reasoning)). The Responses guide's list leaves out `max`, so test before relying on it |

## Background jobs

| Action | Call |
|---|---|
| Create | `POST /v1/responses` with `"background": true` returns `status: "queued"` |
| Poll | `GET /v1/responses/{id}`: queued, in_progress, completed, failed, cancelled, incomplete |
| Stream events | `GET /v1/responses/{id}?stream=true` (lifecycle events; resume with `starting_after`) |
| Cancel | `POST /v1/responses/{id}/cancel` |

- `background` together with `stream` on the create call returns 400.
- Background request bodies are capped at 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes), and anything larger returns 413. Send big inputs as files.

## Files

`POST /v1/files` with `purpose=user_data`: up to 1 GiB per file and 100 GiB per team. Files don't expire unless you set
`expires_after` (3,600 to 2,592,000 seconds).

## Retention

The Terms say content is kept "as needed", with no period stated, and the docs don't say how long stored responses
last. Persist anything you need on your side. Zero data retention needs Meta's sales team and switches off background
requests, server-side history, file uploads, web search and Contributor mode
([ZDR](https://dev.meta.ai/help/policies-and-privacy/zero-data-retention)).

Sources: as linked, checked 2026-10-26.

# Models, prices and limits

## Model ids

From [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models). Confirm with `GET https://api.meta.ai/v1/models`.

| Model | Id | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark | `muse-spark-1.3` | "Recommended for new work"; audio understanding is not fully supported. Older: `-1.2`, `-1.1` |
| Muse Spark (contributor) | `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, `muse-spark-1.2-contributor` | Cheaper; content may be used for training |
| Muse Wonder | `muse-wonder-1.0` | In preview. No contributor version on the Model API |
| SAM 3.1 | `sam-3.1` | The product page writes `sam-3-1` |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0` | See [speech-to-text.md](speech-to-text.md) |
| Muse Image | `muse-image-1.0` | Image generation and editing |

## Prices

From [Pricing and rate limits](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits).

| Model | Input, per 1M tokens | Cached input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Wonder | $4.00 | $0.20 | $20.00 |
| Muse Spark (Standard) | $1.25 | $0.15 | $4.25 |
| Muse Spark (Contributor) | $0.10 | $0.002 | $0.20 |

| Other | Price |
|---|---|
| Web search tool | $2.50 per 1,000 queries |
| Muse Image | $0.01 per image |
| Muse Voice Transcribe | $0.18 per audio hour |
| SAM 3.1 | $2.50 per 1,000 images; $0.20 per 1,000 video frames, with at least 50 frames billed per video request |

## Rate limits (per team, not per key)

| Model | Requests a minute | Tokens a minute |
|---|---|---|
| `muse-wonder-1.0`, `muse-spark-1.3`, `-1.2`, `-1.1` | 3,000 | 4,000,000 |
| `-contributor` ids | 150 | 3,000,000 |
| `sam-3.1` | 3,000 | none |
| `muse-image-1.0` | 150 | none |

- Background responses: 600 submissions a minute per team.
- Voice Transcribe: 256 concurrent streams and 16,000 streams an hour.

## Data use

| Tier | Training on your content | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | No ([data commitments](https://dev.meta.ai/legal/commitments)) | Anything sensitive, confidential or personal |
| Contributor ("Discounted" on the commitments page) | Yes, may be used to train | Non-sensitive work only; the Terms bar sensitive, confidential or personal information (s.6.2) |

Sources: as linked, checked 2026-10-26.

FILE: meta-platform/muse-code.md
URL: https://github.com/ta-amps/ta-amps-hackathon/blob/main/hackathon/meta-platform/muse-code.md
========================================================================

> Unofficial AI-assisted summary, provided "as is" with no warranty. Meta's documentation governs; read [DISCLAIMER.md](../DISCLAIMER.md). As of 2026-10-26.

# Muse Code

Meta's coding agent CLI. Stable release 1.4.13 on Oct 26 ([channel](https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/channels/muse-stable)).

## Install: download, read, then run

The docs ([Muse Code](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code), [quickstart](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/quickstart)) pipe
`https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh` straight into a shell. The script uses bash-only syntax, so if you pipe it, use bash.
Better still, download it, read it and then run it: [../scripts/install-muse-code.sh](../scripts/install-muse-code.sh)
does exactly that.

| What the installer does | Detail |
|---|---|
| Installs to | `${MUSE_INSTALL_DIR:-$HOME/.local/bin}` |
| Edits your shell rc files | Unless `MUSE_NO_MODIFY_PATH` is set |
| Platforms | Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (macOS needs 12 or later on Apple silicon) |
| Auto-update | Hourly, unless `MUSE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1`. Consider setting it while you record a demo |
| Size | The Linux x86 binary is about 400 MB |

The CLI isn't on npm. `@muse-code/sdk` is a separate TypeScript SDK.

## Sandbox (Linux)

From [permissions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/permissions):

- Linux uses a bundled bubblewrap helper. Without a working bubblewrap, every shell command fails as an environment error.
- Inside the sandbox only the workspace and a temp directory are writable. `.git`, `.muse` and `.agents` stay read-only,
  so an agent can't rewrite its own skills or hooks.
- Network modes: `--sandbox-network proxy-only` (default), `restricted` or `unrestricted`.

## Sign-in, billing and Contributor mode

- Sign in through the browser or paste an API key. In CI, `META_API_KEY` is used first, then a stored key, then a browser session ([auth](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/auth)).
- Billing is pay-as-you-go, or a subscription (the docs list Everyday, High, Power and Maximum) ([subscriptions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/subscriptions)).
- **Subscriptions default to Contributor mode**, which lets Meta train on your content. A headless run can have it on if
  the setting was never saved. Pass `--contributor-mode off`, or set `MUSE_CONTRIBUTOR_MODE=0`, on every run that
  touches anything sensitive.

## Headless runs

From [extending](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/extending) and [configuration](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/configuration):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `muse exec --json` | Run headless; JSON Lines events on stdout |
| `--prompt-file <path>` | Take the task from a file |
| `--max-model-steps <n>` | Stop after n model steps |
| `--disable-approval` | Skip approval prompts **but keep the sandbox** (the safe long-run mode) |
| `--approval-mode on-request\|untrusted\|never` | Approval policy |
| `--yolo` | Disables approvals **and the sandbox**, and trusts the workspace. Don't use it |
| `--disable-sandbox` | Turns the sandbox off. Don't use it |
| `--trust-workspace`, `--session-id`, `--approval-judge on\|off` | Other options |

Exit codes: 0 when the turn completes; 1 when it fails or is cancelled (including hitting the step cap); 2 for a usage
error; 130 or 143 on SIGINT or SIGTERM. The default model is `muse-spark-1.2`.

## Configuration

- User settings live in `~/.config/muse/settings.json`, which **must** contain `"schema_version": 1`. No project-level
  settings file is documented.
- `agents.execution_capacity` sets how many agents run at once: 1 to 64, default 8.

## Instructions, skills, hooks, MCP, workflows

| Topic | What the docs say |
|---|---|
| Instruction files | Reads the first that exists of `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.agents/AGENTS.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and only after you trust the workspace |
| Skills | `<repo>/.agents/skills/<skill-id>/SKILL.md`; also scans `.codex/skills` and `.claude/skills`. Frontmatter isn't documented beyond `metadata.display-name` and `allowed-tools` |
| Hooks | Project file `<repo>/.muse/hooks.json`; 17 events including SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop and SessionEnd. **Hooks run outside the sandbox and approvals.** The file format isn't documented |
| MCP | `mcp_servers` in settings; `stdio` or `streamable_http` (url, headers); `mode` `required` (default, aborts the run on failure) or `optional`. **MCP tools aren't sandboxed.** Trusted project `.mcp.json` files load too |
| Workflows | `.agents/workflows/<name>.js`; up to 1,000 child tasks, 16 active; availability depends on build and rollout ([workflows](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/workflows)) |

## Safety checklist

- [ ] Sandbox on; never `--yolo` or `--disable-sandbox`
- [ ] `--contributor-mode off` on anything sensitive
- [ ] `--max-model-steps` set on every headless run
- [ ] Only hooks and MCP servers you wrote or reviewed
- [ ] `MUSE_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1` while recording a demo
- [ ] Keys in the environment or a secret store, never in prompts or files

More: [../agents/muse/README.md](../agents/muse/README.md). Sources: as linked, checked 2026-10-26.

# Open weights and safety tools

## Safety

| Tool | What it is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt Guard 2 | A small classifier for prompt injection and jailbreak attempts | Open weights, gated on Hugging Face with manual approval, so request access early. Unverified here: whether the Model API serves it |

## Data and evaluation

| Tool | What it is |
|---|---|
| [ARE and Gaia2](https://huggingface.co/blog/gaia2) | Meta's agent research environment: simulated worlds with apps, timed and triggered events, and JSON traces |
| [Faiss](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) | Vector similarity search; handy for finding duplicates and related items |
| [Ax](https://github.com/facebook/Ax) | Adaptive experimentation and Bayesian optimization; handy for tuning a few settings against a metric |

## Open-weights models and partner inference

- Meta's open-weights models can be run without a Model API account. The docs list them under
  [open-weight models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/open-weight-models), including
  [Muse Spark Open](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-spark-open) and [Muse Glimmer post-training](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-glimmer/post-training).
  (Linked, not re-read on Oct 26.)
- Partner credits for select participants: Baseten, Modal and Fireworks. See [../event/10-credits.md](../event/10-credits.md).
- Before any fine-tuning that learns from Model API outputs, read the Terms clause that bars training or distilling
  competing models (s.10.1(ix)). See [../event/13-acceptable-use-and-data.md](../event/13-acceptable-use-and-data.md).
- Open-weight model licences carry their own terms, for example attribution requirements for derivatives. Read each
  licence before you ship.

Sources: as linked, checked 2026-10-26 unless marked.

> Unofficial AI-assisted summary, provided "as is" with no warranty. Meta's documentation governs; read [DISCLAIMER.md](../DISCLAIMER.md). As of 2026-10-26.

# Speech to text (Muse Voice Transcribe)

Source: https://dev.meta.ai/docs/speech-to-text, checked 2026-10-26.

## Files

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/transcribe` (optional `?sessionId=…`) |
| Auth | `Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY` |
| Body | `multipart/form-data` with a `request` part (JSON settings) and an `audio` part (the WAV file) |
| `request` fields | `model` (`muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`), `audioEncoding` (`WAV`), `mode` (`PUSH_TO_TALK` default, `ENDPOINTING` or `DIARIZATION`), optional `languageBias` (language names) and `keywords` |
| Audio | RIFF/WAVE, mono, 16-bit PCM, 16 or 24 kHz |
| Limits | 32 MB per request (413 if larger); 10 minutes of audio per request (400 if longer) |
| Response | `sessionId`, `transcript`, `audioDurationMs`, and `turns` (each with `turnId`, `startMs`, `endMs`, `transcript`, and `speaker` in diarization mode). In push-to-talk mode `turns` is empty |
| Accept | `application/json` (default), `text/event-stream` or `text/plain`; anything else returns 406 |
| Price | $0.18 per audio hour |

To convert other audio, the docs use ffmpeg with mono, a 24 kHz rate, 16-bit PCM and stripped metadata:

```bash
ffmpeg -i input.m4a -ac 1 -ar 24000 -c:a pcm_s16le -map_metadata -1 output.wav
```

## Realtime

A WebSocket at `wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime`. Authentication goes in the handshake frame; the Authorization
header is ignored. Limits: 256 concurrent streams and 16,000 streams an hour per team.

## Languages (25)

Arabic, Bengali, Dutch, English, French, German, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Kannada, Korean, Malay,
Mandarin Chinese, Marathi, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish, Tagalog, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese.
Not listed, among others: Nepali, Amharic, Swahili.

## A ready-made client

[../tools/transcribe/](../tools/transcribe/README.md) splits long WAV files into chunks under both limits, sends each,
and stitches a timestamped transcript. Use it only on audio you have the right to use.
